# Vaccination and immunization

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Vaccination and immunization** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Human Health and Diseases fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Vaccination and immunization

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

A **vaccine** is a preparation of antigen — killed, weakened, fragmented or synthesized — that trains the immune system without causing disease. Immunization is the process of becoming protected. The principle is Edward Jenner's (cowpox → smallpox, 1796): a mild first encounter produces memory cells, so the real pathogen meets a fast, massive secondary response.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — how a vaccine becomes protection (study in this order)**

| Step | Event | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vaccine antigen delivered (injection / oral) | Antigen reaches lymphoid tissue |
| 2 | B and T cells with matching receptors activate | Clonal expansion |
| 3 | Antibodies produced; antigen cleared | Mild or no symptoms |
| 4 | Memory B and T cells form | Long-term armed state |
| 5 | Real pathogen arrives months or years later | Secondary response in 1–2 days — pathogen destroyed before disease |

**Types of vaccines — classified with examples**

| Type | What it contains | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Live attenuated | Weakened living pathogen | BCG (TB), MMR, oral polio (OPV) | Strong, long-lasting immunity; caution in immune-suppressed people |
| Killed / inactivated | Pathogen killed by heat or chemicals | Injectable polio (IPV), rabies, whole-cell pertussis | Safer, but usually needs boosters |
| Toxoid | Inactivated toxin | Tetanus, diphtheria | Trains the body against the toxin, not the bacterium |
| Subunit / conjugate | Purified protein or sugar-protein piece | Hepatitis B (surface antigen), Hib, pneumococcal | No live material at all — safest for the immune-compromised |
| mRNA / vector | Instructions for cells to make one viral protein | COVID-19 mRNA vaccines | Newest class; rapid development |

**Active vs passive immunization — the two ways to protect**

| Feature | Active immunization (vaccination) | Passive immunization |
|---|---|---|
| What is given | Antigen | Ready-made antibodies |
| Example | Polio drops, BCG, tetanus toxoid | Antivenom for snake bite, antitetanus serum, colostrum IgA |
| Onset of protection | Days to weeks (body must respond) | Immediate |
| Duration | Years — memory cells persist | Short — antibodies decay, no memory |
| Use case | Routine prevention | Emergency after exposure, or people who cannot be vaccinated |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A child receives DPT at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. The first dose is the primary response — antibodies appear after about a week and fade. The second and third doses act as boosters: each triggers a bigger, faster IgG response and a larger memory pool. That is why the schedule has three doses, and why a tetanus booster every few years keeps protection high. A person stepped on a rusty nail who was never vaccinated gets **antitetanus serum** — passive immunization, immediate but temporary.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Define vaccine and immunization. (2) Classify vaccine types with one example each. (3) Distinguish active from passive immunization in four points. (4) Why are boosters needed for killed vaccines but less so for live attenuated ones? (5) Name two diseases of the national immunization schedule (BCG — tuberculosis; OPV — polio).

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Vaccines present antigen safely; the immune system responds, then remembers. Killed and subunit vaccines need boosters; live attenuated ones usually do not; passive immunization is borrowed protection for emergencies. **Self-check:** can you draw the two-curve antibody graph and label primary vs secondary?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Principle: harmless antigen → primary response → memory cells → rapid secondary response on real infection — the memory mechanism IS the answer.
Trick 2: Vaccine types: killed/inactivated (polio Salk), live attenuated (BCG, oral polio Sabin), toxoid (tetanus), subunit/recombinant (Hepatitis B) — one example each.
Trick 3: Passive immunisation: antivenom, immunoglobulin shots — immediate protection without memory.
Trick 4: National programmes: Pulse Polio, BCG at birth, DPT schedule — quote one for the applied mark.
